title: Mutual Fund Challenge
subtitle: Put money in a fund, watch made-up years go by, and see what units, dips and fees do to it.
open.hint: Pick a fund, invest a lump sum or a monthly SIP, and compare.
p1.hint: Read this, play with the numbers, then continue.
p3.hint: Choose how the money goes in, how much, and for how long.
r1.title: How it went
r1.hint: Your made-up years in one picture.
r2.title: The ups and downs
r2.hint: Prices rise and fall. See how that looked, and what your money bought.
r3.title: What it cost
r3.hint: Every fund takes a yearly cost. Compare all four in the same market.
r4.title: Other ways it could have gone
r4.hint: Your market was one of many. These are 500 others.
r5.title: Fund or ETF?
r5.hint: Two ways to buy, with one thing in common.
r6.title: Check what you learned
r6.hint: Six short questions, one at a time.
learn.pool.title: Many small amounts, one big pool
learn.pool.body: A fund collects money from many people. A manager buys small pieces of many companies with it. Each person owns units of the pool.
learn.nav.title: The unit price, called NAV
learn.nav.body: NAV is the fund's total value divided by its units. The units you get are your money divided by the NAV.
learn.calc.nav: NAV, the price of one unit
pick.intro: Four made-up funds. None is best for everyone. Look at what each one holds and what it costs.
pick.more: What it holds, and what a year might look like
pick.year: A typical year, after cost: ₹10,000 ends between {low} and {high}
pick.etf: Bought on the exchange at a market price. Each purchase costs {tc} of the amount.
fund.index_basket.what: Follows a list of many companies. It does not try to beat the list.
fund.active_growth.what: A manager picks companies to try to beat the list, and charges more for trying.
fund.active_growth.holds: Fewer companies, picked by the manager.
fund.sector_focus.what: Holds companies from one industry only.
fund.sector_focus.holds: One industry. If it struggles, the whole fund feels it.
fund.index_etf.what: Follows a list of companies, like the Index Basket Fund, but trades on an exchange like a share.
fund.index_etf.holds: A similar list, bought at a market price during the day.
plan.sip: A SIP: the same amount every month
plan.summary: You will put in {total} in all, in {fund}.
result.title: What happened in this market
result.market: One made-up market. Dips and booms come from the same engine as the other games.
chart.value: Your units' value, and what you put in
chart.units: Units your money bought each month
futures.title: 500 other possible futures for the same plan
futures.note: Simulation based on made-up numbers. Not a prediction.
compare.title: All four funds in the same market
compare.note: Same market, same luck. The differences come from each fund's swings and costs. This is one market, not a ranking.
fee.title: What the yearly cost does
fee.formula: A lump sum after n years = amount × (1 + yearly growth − yearly cost)^years. A bigger cost, every year, compounds against you.
etf.title: How an ETF differs from a mutual fund
etf.row.boughtEtf: A market price, any time the exchange is open
etf.row.throughFund: The fund company or a platform
etf.row.costEtf: Often low for index-style, plus a trading cost each time
etf.row.smallEtf: Possible, but each buy is a trade
etf.same: What is the same: what is inside the fund decides the risk.
never: No fund is best for everyone. Which suits you depends on how long you can wait, how much you will add, and what it costs.
assume.note: Each fund has a made-up growth rate, swing and yearly cost, shown in assumptions.json. Prices move with calm, boom and crash periods.
check.title: Check what you learned
note.result: You put in {invested}. After {years} years in this market, your units were worth {value}: {gain} ({pct}).
note.sip.units: The unit price was lowest in month {cheap}, at {nav}, so {amount} bought {units} units. It was highest in month {dear}, at {navHigh}, where the same money bought only {unitsHigh}.
note.sip.average: Your average cost per unit was {avg}, below the plain average price of {avgNav}. You bought more when it was low.
note.dip: At its worst, the unit price was {dd} below an earlier peak. Anyone who sold then locked in that fall.
note.cost: The fund's yearly cost took about {drag} over {years} years, which is {pct} of what your units ended up worth.
note.etf.trading: Each purchase cost a small trading fee. Over {n} purchases, that came to {total}.
note.vsIndex.above: In this market, {name} ended {amount} above the {index}. In other markets it could be different.
note.vsIndex.below: In this market, {name} ended {amount} below the {index}. In other markets it could be different.
note.think.loss: In about {chance} of 500 other possible futures, you ended below what you put in. What would that mean for your goal?
note.think.neverZero: The chance of ending below what you put in looks small here, but it is never zero.
note.think.sector: A sector fund holds one industry. If that industry struggles, little else cushions the fall.
note.think.active: An active fund tries to beat the list, and charges more for trying. Compare its cost with what it earned.
note.think.etf: An ETF is bought like a share, so each purchase is a trade with a cost. How often would you buy?
note.think.noBest: Try another fund or another way of investing. Which parts changed your result, and which were luck?
check.f1.prompt: You put {money} into a fund when the NAV is {nav1}. How many units do you get? Type a number.
check.f1.hint: Your money divided by the NAV.
check.f2.prompt: Next month the NAV falls to {nav2}. How many units does {money} buy now? Type a number.
check.f2.hint: Your money divided by the new, lower NAV.
check.f2.explain: {money} divided by {nav2} is {u2} units. The lower price bought more.
check.f3.prompt: Why does a SIP buy more units when the NAV falls?
check.f3.opt.a: The same rupees are divided by a lower price
check.f3.opt.b: A SIP always makes a profit
check.f3.fb.b: A SIP cannot promise a profit. It only spreads your buying over time.
check.f3.hint: Money divided by a smaller number gives a bigger number.
check.f3.explain: The same money divided by a lower NAV gives more units.
check.f4.prompt: A lump sum of {P} grows {gross} a year before cost, for {yrs} years. How much less does it end at with a yearly cost of {feeB} than with {feeA}? Type a number in rupees.
check.f4.hint: Grow it at the growth rate minus each cost, then subtract the two end amounts.
check.f4.explain: At a cost of {feeA} it ends at {endA}. At {feeB} it ends at {endB}. The gap is {gap}.
check.f5.prompt: What is the main difference between an ETF and a typical mutual fund?
check.f5.opt.a: An ETF is bought and priced during the day, like a share
check.f5.opt.b: An ETF holds only one company
check.f5.opt.c: An ETF is safer because it is on an exchange
check.f5.opt.d: An ETF is not a pool of many things
check.f5.fb.c: Being on an exchange does not make it safer. What is inside decides the risk.
check.f5.hint: Think about the day-end price compared with a price that moves during the day.
check.f5.explain: The main difference is how it is bought and priced. What is inside decides the risk.
check.f6.prompt: Asha asks which fund is the best. What is a good reply?
check.f6.opt.a: None is best for everyone. It depends on time, amounts and cost
check.f6.opt.b: The one with the highest yearly cost
check.f6.opt.c: The one that finished on top in this game
check.f6.fb.b: A higher cost is only a higher cost. It does not buy better results.
check.f6.fb.c: One market is one roll of the dice. The same fund can finish lower in another market.
check.f6.fb.d: No type of fund is always best. It depends on your time, your amounts and the cost.
check.f6.hint: Remember the last line under the comparison.
check.f6.explain: No fund is best for everyone. The right one depends on time, amounts and cost.
